title: Ontario Home EV Charger Rebate 2026: What Is Open
desc: Ontario has no open home EV charger rebate in 2026. Toronto's HELP loan covers a Level 2 charger, and the overnight electricity rate is the saving that applies everywhere.
h1: Ontario Home EV Charger Rebates in 2026
lead: If you own a house in Ontario and want a charger in the garage, we could not find a rebate you can apply for today. We read the provincial, federal and city programs on October 4, 2026. This page says what each one covers, what the work needs by law, and where the real savings are.
cards_heading: What we checked for Ontario home chargers
cards_intro: Each card names the official page we read. A charger is not on any of the provincial lists.

cards.title: Save on Energy
cards.note: The province's home programs are Home Renovation Savings, Peak Perks, the Energy Affordability Program and two advice tools. None of them pays for an EV charger.

cards.title: Toronto HELP loan
cards.note: A Level 2 charging station is on the City of Toronto's list of eligible improvements. The loan is repaid on your property tax bill. Rates were last posted to September 30, 2026, so ask the City for the current ones.

cards.title: Federal ZEVIP
cards.note: Natural Resources Canada funds chargers in public places, workplaces, fleets and multi-unit buildings. It does not fund individual homeowners, and its application streams are closed.

cards.title: Federal EV Affordability Program
cards.note: Runs from February 16, 2026 to March 31, 2031 or until the money runs out. It helps with buying or leasing an eligible vehicle, not with the charger.

cards.title: Federal iZEV
cards.note: The old vehicle incentive ended March 31, 2025 and never paid for chargers.

after_cards: We have not read every local distributor's pages. If your bill comes from a smaller utility, ask it whether a charger pilot is running, and we will add anything that opens.
sections: Where the saving is: the overnight rate

With no rebate, the biggest saving comes from when you charge. The Ontario Energy Board sets the prices every November 1. Since November 1, 2025, the Ultra-Low Overnight plan charges 3.9 cents per kilowatt-hour from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. every day. Time-of-Use off-peak is 9.8 cents. A car that needs 60 kWh to fill costs about $2.34 at the overnight price and about $5.88 at the off-peak price, before delivery charges.

The catch is the weekday on-peak price on that plan: 39.1 cents from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. A household that cooks, runs the dryer and the dishwasher in that window can lose what the car saves. Any Ontario distributor can switch you, and the plan suits people who can plug in after 11 p.m. and move other loads out of the early evening.
What the work needs by law

Charger wiring in Ontario is work for a licensed electrician. The Electrical Safety Authority says a licensed electrical contractor must file a notification of work before starting, and the contractor gets a Certificate of Acceptance once the work passes. After a 2023 blitz in Toronto, ESA reported more than 400 incidents of charger installs done with no permit. Ask for a copy of the notification and keep the certificate.

The wiring is where costs vary. A charger needs spare capacity on your electrical service. Ask the electrician for a load calculation before you buy anything. A smaller charger, or a charger that shares power with the rest of the house, can avoid a panel upgrade in some homes. We do not publish a typical price here because Ontario quotes depend on the distance from the panel and the age of the service, and we have no official figure to cite.
Toronto's loan, and what it does not do

Toronto is the one place in this list where a charger gets help from a public program, and it is financing. The City's Home Energy Loan Program accepts a Level 2 charging station alongside heat pumps, windows and solar, up to $125,000 and no more than 10% of your assessed value, plus a 2% administrative charge. It is repaid over your tax bill and stays with the property. Whether it beats your bank line of credit depends on the rate on the day you apply.

The federal ZEVIP funds chargers at multi-unit buildings, workplaces and public sites, not at single homes. If you live in a condo, the first step is the board and the building's electrical capacity, not a rebate form. Renters should get the landlord's agreement before any wiring is done.
Pair it with money that does exist

If the garage visit is already booked, ask the electrician about the panel at the same time as other upgrades. A heat pump or an electric water heater adds load as well. Home Renovation Savings pays for heat pumps, insulation, windows and water heaters, and the $125 smart thermostat rebate is separate. See the links below for those programs.
claim_heading: How to add a home charger in Ontario
claim_steps: Hire a licensed electrical contractor and ask for a load calculation first.
Choose a charger size your panel can carry; ask about power sharing if it is tight.
Confirm the contractor files the ESA notification of work before starting.
Ask your distributor to put you on the Ultra-Low Overnight plan if you charge after 11 p.m.
In Toronto, ask the City about a HELP loan before you pay by cash or card.
Keep the ESA Certificate of Acceptance with your house papers.

faq: Is there a home EV charger rebate in Ontario?
We found none open in 2026. Save on Energy lists no charger program, and federal ZEVIP does not fund individual homeowners.
Can I use a Toronto HELP loan for a charger?
Yes. The City lists Level 2 charging stations as eligible. It is a loan repaid on your property tax bill, not a rebate, so check the current rate.
Does the federal EV program pay for the charger?
No. The Electric Vehicle Affordability Program helps with buying or leasing an eligible vehicle. It does not pay for the charger or the wiring.
Do I need a permit to install a home charger in Ontario?
The licensed electrical contractor files a notification of work with the Electrical Safety Authority before starting and gets a certificate when the work is accepted. Do not hire anyone who skips it.
Is the Ultra-Low Overnight plan worth it for an EV?

At 3.9 cents overnight against 9.8 cents off-peak, a 60 kWh charge costs about $2.34 against $5.88. The on-peak rate of 39.1 cents on weekday evenings is the risk, so it suits homes that can shift other use.
